# Exact obstructions to two single-step localizations after Schwarz symmetry

These statements concern the conditional Schwarz reduction in
candidate 5f965fa405cfb1cb (candidate 5f965fa405cfb1cb).
They are stronger preservation obstructions, not counterexamples to OC.
The first applies directly to the exact source force/tensor system;
the second tests radial level selection in an explicit symmetric
convex body with an actual objective-one rank-restricted stress.

## 1. A common lower-dimensional affine support cannot retain the tensor

Let `nu` be any finite nonnegative measure on labeled points `(i,z,x)`.
Let the label normals be fixed vectors `U=u_i`. Suppose

`integral U dnu=0`,
`integral z U^T dnu=0`,
`integral x U^T dnu=Q`.                                    (1)

If the continuous support has the form

`x in c+Bz+L`,

where `L` is a fixed linear subspace, then

`range(Q) subset L`.                                       (2)

Indeed the constant and affine-base terms vanish in the last integral
by the first two equations of (1). Its remaining integrand has
continuous coordinate in `L`, so every column of the integral lies
in `L`. This proof allows arbitrary densities, atoms, different base
weights, and any number or direction of cap labels.

For the normal source law after Schwarz symmetry,

`Q=sum_i Psi_i u_i u_i^T`.

Its rank is exactly the dimension of the span of the positive-hinge
cap normals. Thus a single common affine needle or flat, even after
an arbitrary continuous affine shear in the base, cannot lower that
dimension while preserving all the force and tensor equations with
their original right-hand side. This obstruction does not apply to
a mixture of differently oriented localizations, or to a localization
which changes the tensor it is asked to preserve.

## 2. One radial level cannot preserve both the force and the tensor

Consider the already conditionally symmetric triangle

`C={(v,w):0<=v<=1, |w|<=1-v}`.

Here `n=0,d=2`, `V` is the v-axis, the perpendicular dimension is
`m=1`, and the source mass is one. Its projected density is

`f(v)=2(1-v)`, `0<=v<=1`.

Put `h=1-1/sqrt(2)`. The two opposite selected caps are
`H_+={v>=h}` and `H_-={v<=h}`. Both have source mass one half.
Their unit normals are `+1,-1` in `V`, and their hinges are

`Psi_+=1/(6sqrt(2))`,
`Psi_-=2/3-5/(6sqrt(2))`,
`Psi_++Psi_-=(2-sqrt(2))/3`.                                (3)

For example, the upper formula follows by integrating
`2(1-v)(v-h)` from h to one; the lower follows from the mean
`E v=1/3` and the difference of the two hinges.

This is an actual objective-one normal system for a rank-restricted
whole-line hinge minimum. Among two opposite unit-normal caps,
whole-line coverage requires thresholds `a<=b`. Pointwise

`(v-a)_+ +(b-v)_+ >= |v-(a+b)/2|`.

The expected absolute deviation is minimized at its unique median h.
The displayed caps attain that minimum. Therefore the two-cap
rank-restricted hinge value is constant at (3) for every budget
`tau>=1/2`; the union bound makes smaller budgets infeasible.
At a regular `tau>1/2`, take budget multipliers zero, coverage
multiplier one, balanced circuit weights `(1/2,1/2)`, and contact
`(h,0)`. The mass and continuous moment identities hold exactly;
perpendicular moments vanish by reflection symmetry. Its source
force is zero and its scalar source tensor is the last value in (3).
No unrestricted two-dimensional global minimization is needed or
claimed here.

The radial layer-cake representation of the projected density is

`f(v)=2 integral_0^1 1_{[0,1-t]}(v) dt`.                    (4)

Choose a single level `t`, and allow its uniform interval law to be
rescaled to total mass one. If it is to preserve the two selected cap
masses, or equivalently the zero normal force, its median must remain
h. This forces

`1-t=2h=2-sqrt(2)`.

At that unique level the sum of the selected hinges is the absolute
deviation about the midpoint of a uniform interval, namely

`(1-t)/4=(2-sqrt(2))/4`,                                   (5)

which is strictly smaller than the tensor in (3), by exactly
`(2-sqrt(2))/12`. Thus no single radial level, even after arbitrary
positive rescaling of its mass, preserves both the force and the
original tensor. There is also no uniform interval contained in
the original projection `[0,1]` which does so: its midpoint would
have to be h, its length would be at most `2h`, and (5) is then
the largest possible hinge sum.

If every selected hinge is required separately, the obstruction is
even immediate from (3): a uniform interval bisected by the selected
cut has equal upper and lower hinges, whereas the two values in
(3) differ. Allowing a nonuniform tent density would retain the
original hidden slice exponent rather than furnish a uniform-measure
dimension deletion; such a weighted replacement is not excluded.

## 3. Dropping a perpendicular dimension while retaining the entire marginal

There is a separate simple exponent obstruction. Suppose a symmetric
body has slice radius `R(p)` which is positive, affine, and nonconstant
on a segment of its real projection. Its projected density is
`f(p)=kappa_m R(p)^m`. If `m>=2`, a convex body with only `m-1`
perpendicular dimensions and exactly this same projected density
would require `f^(1/(m-1))` to be concave by Brunn-Minkowski. But

`f^(1/(m-1))=kappa_m^(1/(m-1)) R^(m/(m-1))`

is strictly convex on that segment. Such a convex realization is
therefore impossible. For `m=1`, deletion to zero perpendicular
dimensions would require the uniform density of a projected set;
a nonconstant affine slice density is not of that form.

This last statement preserves the entire marginal, which is stronger
than preserving finitely many cap constraints. The single-level
calculation in Section 2 instead isolates a finite force/tensor
incompatibility. Together with (2), these results explain precisely
why conditional Schwarz symmetry does not by itself authorize a
single needle, a single radial level, or a uniform dimension deletion.
No general localization theorem is disproved or presumed.
